planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set out only after soil has warmed, since this low spreading South American native resents cold, wet ground.

directions: Clasping heliotrope forms a low, sprawling mat of fuzzy gray-green leaves topped by curled, scorpioid clusters of small violet-purple flowers from late spring through fall. It thrives in hot, lean, well-drained soil and shrugs off drought once roots are established, making it a reliable edging or groundcover for xeriscape beds. In mild southern zones it behaves as a woody-based perennial; farther north it is simply grown as a heat-loving annual. Shear lightly after the first flush to encourage denser rebloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown rosettes in spring into sharply drained, gravelly soil well away from foot traffic, since the tall flower spikes open at dusk and are best enjoyed from a seating area nearby.

directions: This Sonoran Desert native forms an evergreen rosette of narrow, fibrous, gray-green leaves and sends up slender spikes bearing pendulous, cream to pale-green, bell-shaped flowers that open in the evening and release a sweet fragrance to attract night-flying pollinators. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs almost no supplemental irrigation outside of the hottest, driest stretches of summer. Give it full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, and avoid overhead watering that can rot the crown. Established clumps slowly produce offsets that can be divided for propagation.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring into lean, fast-draining soil, and withhold summer irrigation once roots are established to keep growth compact and flowering strong.

directions: Native to Spain and Portugal, this evergreen subshrub carries felted, gray-green leaves and whorls of soft lilac-purple, hooded flowers stacked along upright stems through summer, giving a softer color echo of the more familiar yellow-flowered Phlomis fruticosa. It is tough and drought tolerant once rooted in, needing only sharp drainage and a sunny spot to thrive in hot, dry gardens. Cut back hard in late winter to keep the habit tidy, since older wood can become leggy. It pairs well with other Mediterranean dry-garden plants like lavender and rosemary.

planting.note: Divide and replant in early spring into gritty, well-drained soil, tucking crowns into rock crevices or wall tops where excess moisture drains away quickly.

directions: This hybrid soapwort forms a low, spreading mound of narrow dark-green leaves smothered through much of the summer in small, star-shaped, deep pink flowers, making it a long-blooming staple for rock gardens, troughs, and dry stone walls. It tolerates lean, gritty soil and poor fertility far better than rich garden beds, and good drainage is more important to its longevity than feeding. Shear the mound back by about a third after the first big flush to tidy it and coax a second round of bloom. Established clumps are easily lifted and divided every few years to keep them vigorous.

planting.note: Plant a grafted sapling in full sun in spring, staking young trees in windy sites since the wood is somewhat brittle until well established.

directions: 'Frisia' is the golden-leaved form of black locust, holding bright yellow foliage from spring leaf-out through fall color change, with the strongest tone developing in full sun. Like the species it fixes its own nitrogen and tolerates poor, dry, or disturbed soils, making it a fast-growing choice for difficult sites, though it flowers less heavily than the green wild type. Watch for root suckers and prune out any green-leaved reversion shoots that arise from the rootstock below the graft. Thorny young growth and brittle limbs in storms are worth keeping in mind when siting it near walkways.

planting.note: Plant a grafted standard in spring in any well-drained soil; its neat, self-contained crown needs little formative pruning once the graft union has healed.

directions: This grafted cultivar forms a dense, rounded, umbrella-like crown without a dominant central leader, growing far more slowly and compactly than the wild species and almost never producing the fragrant flower clusters typical of the type. Its tidy, symmetrical silhouette and lack of significant thorns make it a popular choice for small street trees and formal courtyard plantings where the thorny, suckering habit of ordinary black locust would be unwelcome. It tolerates poor, compacted, or dry urban soils with ease. Remove any vigorous shoots arising below the graft, as these revert to the ordinary tree form.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun and withhold summer irrigation entirely once established, since wet roots in warm weather are the most common cause of failure.

directions: A hybrid between Fremontodendron californicum and F. mexicanum, 'Ken Taylor' grows lower and spreads wider than the straight species while producing an especially heavy, extended show of large, deep golden-orange, saucer-shaped flowers from spring into summer. Like its parents it demands lean, fast-draining soil and absolutely no summer water once established, making it best suited to dry-garden and California native plantings rather than irrigated borders. Because the bristly stellate hairs covering the leaves and stems are a strong skin and eye irritant, always wear gloves and eye protection when pruning or handling it. It is propagated by cuttings rather than seed, since the hybrid does not come true from seed.

planting.note: Sow into deep plug trays or direct into scree beds, since this rosette-forming alpine develops a long taproot early and resents root disturbance when transplanting.

directions: Native to Rocky Mountain alpine and subalpine slopes, this short-lived perennial forms a tight basal rosette of narrow, hairy leaves topped by large, nearly stemless, lavender-blue daisy flowers with sunny yellow centers in early summer. It needs the same sharp drainage and lean, mineral soil it finds in its native scree and gravel slopes, and will quickly rot in rich, moisture-retentive garden soil. It is a classic choice for alpine troughs, scree beds, and rock gardens at elevation, but may be short-lived in warm, humid lowland climates. Established plants often self-sow modestly where conditions suit them.
